data.title: Trump Vs Zelensky, From the Screen to the Streets, Gen Z protests from Paris to Dehli
data.description:
In India, the Cockroach movement felt the crushing boot of the state this week. Thousands of Gen Z protesters were rounded up and detained in sports stadiums and community halls turned into makeshift detention centres, while the movement’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, was arrested on arrival. A mass demonstration over alleged voter fraud was effectively crushed before it could begin.And Abdijeet has been detained again todayNarendra Modi’s government says the measures were necessary to protect civilians in the capital. But he now faces accusations of choosing repression over democracy, with the UN Human Rights Office urging authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly. 
 
 
 
It’s been a week of blame games and accusations of betrayal in Ukraine with President Zelensky speaking of his personal hurt at President Trump’s decision to make a diesel deal with the Kremlin ahead of the US Mid term elections calling it “weak”, suggesting Trump had chosen, “the other side”. Trump meanwhile made clear he wants Zelensky replaced, and warned him against striking Russian refineries AND announced an energy ceasefire, declaring it to have been agreed by both sides but which went nowhere. President Zelensky continued to search for solidarity and a solution in Europe.

data.title: 'US tilting toward Russia: Europeans are standing more and more solidly with Zelensky'
data.description: As transatlantic relations confront renewed geopolitical uncertainty, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves delivers a pointed assessment of Washington's shifting approach to Russia's war on Ukraine and the profound implications for European security. At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental question: can Europe develop the political unity, strategic independence and military capabilities necessary to defend its interests in an increasingly unpredictable international order?  Ilves response: "If there's any time for Europe to begin to act as Europe and not as being strictly self-interested, then this is the time for it."

data.title: Sally Rooney's books no longer sold in UK over support for banned pro-Palestinian group
data.description: Irish novelist Sally ⁠Rooney's books will ​no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties ​to support Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organisation, Rooney and her publisher said on Wednesday. The bestselling author, known for novels including "Normal People" and "Conversations with ​Friends", has ‌been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, including after ⁠it was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.

data.title: Argentine demonstration over education cuts ends in clashes
data.description: Argentine demonstrators clashed with police on Thursday at a major protest in Buenos Aires over budget-slashing President Javier Milei's higher education spending. The main demonstration outside parliament by thousands of university students and staff, trade unionists and opposition activists remained peaceful. But dozens of mostly hooded demonstrators who broke away from the crowd lobbed stones and other projectiles at the police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons.

data.title: Embattled new White House Press Secretary Zacharia 'let go' from her role
data.description: A White House Press official said Friday that Secretary ​Katie Zacharia was "let go" from her role after US President Donald Trump signaled she was on her way out, a week after he picked her for the post. Zacharia's credentials as an attorney had come under scrutiny and she admitted to not having passed the bar in an interview with Fox News on Thursday.

data.title: India detains top 'cockroach' leader as hundreds protest in capital
data.description: Indian police detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Abhijeet Dipke on Friday ahead of fresh protests demanding the removal of the country's election chief, the youth-led movement said in a social media post. Dipke, 31, was detained shortly before a rally called by the online movement in the heart of New Delhi where hundreds of protesters marched on Friday evening, despite heavy security measures. FRANCE 24's Navodita Kumari reports from New Delhi, India.

data.title: Zelensky hails "real leaders" in Europe, blasts Trump's diesel deal with Russia
data.description: Ukrainian ​President Volodymyr Zelensky took aim on Friday at US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in talks, calling Moscow's stance a "parody" of peace negotiations. At a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskiy said Russia did not want peace. He added that Ukraine was still experiencing disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system. FRANCE 24's Europe Editor Armen Georgian reports from Brussels.

data.title: France braces for massive protests: Yellow Vests to join students on Saturday
data.description: After weeks of student protests, France is set to be swept by broader, nationwide demonstrations on Saturday. The country's Yellow Vest movement – which eight years ago staged street protests against President Emmanuel Macron – has appealed to teachers, workers, pensioners and farmers, as well as students, in an online call spread through social media. The prospect of the two movements merging poses a big challenge to the government, as FRANCE 24’s Shirli Sitbon reports.

data.title: REPLAY: Ukraine's Zelensky holds presser in Brussels
data.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Friday urged European leaders to maintain their support for Kyiv and warned against easing sanctions on Russia. data.title: Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)
data.description: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power. Introduction by Luke Kennard I have an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress. On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”. Men were portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining. Continue reading...

data.title: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
data.description: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said . “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify . A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. Continue reading...

data.title: A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese
data.description: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas As I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …” The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit. Continue reading...

data.title: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
data.description: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam. Aditya’s suggested reading: To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair. For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books. To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian. Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak . Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch. Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party For more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series. And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, read this paper based on data from the Bank of England. Finally, on the Spectator, read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in the Guardian: Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia? Continue reading...

data.title: The Audacity: this witty tech-bro takedown from a Succession writer is packed with glorious one-liners
data.description: Jonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call Saul Many of us yearn for the return of an analogue world, but it’s never coming back. You can’t buy potato waffles without a QR code. I had to arrange an IRL bank appointment for my mother to check her balance, and it took, I don’t know, 100 days? A friend of mine has boycotted WhatsApp, but I can’t tell you how that’s going because we haven’t spoken in a year. Watching The Audacity (from Thursday, HBO Max) this week, I was shaken by how much of our dystopia can be traced to a small number of men in Silicon Valley. Their products and platforms, an expression of their shortfalls as much as their skills, have reshaped our world more seismically than any political party. Their power-brokering has turned a small collection of towns and villages south of San Francisco into a modern-day Camelot. Continue reading...

data.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
data.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community  still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisis
data.description: The author talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novel For a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers. There Are Rivers in the Sky , which follows a single raindrop from ancient Nineveh to the River Tigris in 2018, was one of the UK’s bestselling literary novels last year. The Island of Missing Trees , a love story set in post-colonial Cyprus and contemporary London, was shortlisted for the Women’s prize in 2022, and 10 Minutes 38 seconds in This Strange World , narrated by a murdered sex worker in Istanbul, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2019. Last December she was elected president of the Royal Society of Literature. It would be tempting to say she is on a roll, but Shafak’s reputation and readership have been steadily growing for more than 20 years and spanning as many books, of which 14 are novels. In a 2017 Ted Talk , which has been viewed more than 6.4m times, she describes herself as an Istanbulite, “a European by birth and by choice” and a Londoner for many years. “I like to think of myself as a global soul, as a world citizen, a nomad and an itinerant storyteller.” Her novels sweep confidently across centuries and continents, taking in politics, history, feminism and ecology, typically with a dash of magic realism or mysticism. Continue reading...

data.title: Houthi conflict casts shadow as Saudi Arabia scales back sporting pipe dreams
data.description: A match delayed by missile attack warnings is not what Cristiano Ronaldo and co signed up for but it’s the new reality; the Saudi sporting juggernaut is stalling Cristiano Ronaldo grabbed the scarf in the colours of the Saudi Arabian flag and waved it at the sparse but enthusiastic crowd, who responded with rapturous cheers. It was a gesture of defiance rather than a victory salute, encapsulating the Saudi equivalent of “Keep calm and carry on”. Monday night’s Asian Champions League Elite game between Al-Nassr and the Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana had ended with a 3-1 win for the Saudi club coached by Ange Postecoglou, with Ronaldo, supported by Sadio Mané, scoring, the smattering of star names indicative of the lure of the Saudi Pro League. Yet this isn’t quite how Ronaldo and co would have anticipated life in Riyadh. The meagre attendance aside, Monday’s game was delayed by a threat of missile attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. A safety warning issued 15 minutes before kick-off came two days after 13 people died and more than 300 were wounded by Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport. Continue reading...

data.description: The film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirs I watched the extraordinary new Guardian-produced documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor the other night, and I have struggled to stop thinking about it ever since. The film’s title comes from a Hebrew military term for collateral damage, and it consists of eye-opening interviews with two dozen Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers sitting in darkness, often on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, their voices “digitally altered to disguise their identities”. At one point, Abraham asks one of the soldiers a remarkably blunt question. Continue reading...

data.title: French schoolchildren have been treated like violent criminals – for telling the truth | Rokhaya Diallo
data.description: To protest against the shameful conditions in some French schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not As a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part in protests against a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police response unleashed on student protesters in France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home. A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maël lost the sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedly at groups of secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.” Accounts from children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences. Continue reading...

data.title: Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland
data.description: The old certainties have gone. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in this new and dangerous world Donald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion. Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered an on-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights. Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist US midterms: Trump, war and America’s future On Thursday, 5 November join Jonathan Freedland, Devika Bhat, Professor Adam Smith in London and David Smith and leading US commentator Tara Setmayer live from the US to discuss the results and their implications for the future of Trump, the US and global politics. Book tickets here or at guardian.live Continue reading...

data.title: Women just want to work out in peace. Why all the thigh-rubbing lechery? | Emma Beddington
data.description: On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious I’ve spent the morning doing Shane Gillis’s work: checking out women in the gym. If you’ve avoided Gillis thus far, apologies for enlightening you – he’s a “comedian” who recently told a “joke” on Saturday Night Live that began: “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dressed like whores now.” Well, reporting for duty from the weight room, here’s the clothing tally: eight women in leggings and T-shirts; six in T-shirts and trackie bottoms; five in shorts and vest tops; one in a crop top and leggings. It’s not exactly the Folies Bergère – there’s not much, I would have thought, to cause Gillis to blush. But maybe I’m wrong – how undressed, exactly, constitutes whorish? Is a glimpse of a female forearm a distracting provocation? Should we pull up our socks to avoid inflaming male passions with our slutty ankles when we’re doing step-ups? Continue reading...

data.title: As King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know that Winston Churchill admitted to imperial plunder 90 years ago | Kenneth Mohammed
data.description: Modern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on the vast wealth taken away For us in the Caribbean, there is something surreal about Britain’s renewed nostalgia over empire. As Britain’s monarch prepares to visit the Caribbean , and at a time when we in the former colonies are demanding to have a serious reckoning with slavery and reparations , UK politicians are invoking a dumbed-down distortion of history. Rewriting the facts: the Reform MP Robert Jenrick has argued that colonies owed Britain a “ debt of gratitude ” for the institutions empire bequeathed them. Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former minister in a Conservative government, has described British colonialism as “one of the greatest civilising, prosperity-creating forces the world has ever seen”. The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, has disputed colonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations, former colonies should repay Britain for the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts. Continue reading...

The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, has disputed colonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations, former colonies should repay Britain for the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts. data.title: The Letby case inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald
data.description: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyone Mark McDonald is a barrister representing Lucy Letby I have been Lucy Letby’s barrister for the past two years. I have spent thousands of hours going through the evidence, speaking to experts and examining what happened to the babies who died or became seriously unwell on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. I have worked with nearly 30 experts, including internationally recognised specialists in neonatology, pathology, insulin, statistics and other fields. It may be to some an inconvenient truth, but I am convinced that Letby is innocent, and her convictions represent one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British legal history. That means she was failed by the police, the NHS, the criminal justice system and, importantly, a plethora of experts who simply got it wrong. My work on the case has also raised wider concerns about the evidence and conclusions surrounding the deaths on the neonatal unit, and what the lessons being drawn from this case will mean for doctors and nurses in neonatal medicine. Mark McDonald is a criminal defence and human rights barrister specialising in miscarriages of justice Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? data.title: The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
data.description: Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed , in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill. The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year . This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing . The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last. data.title: The Guardian view on Winnie-the-Pooh: now we are 100 | Editorial
data.description: He may have been eclipsed by the more progressive Paddington of late, but AA Milne’s creation is not just a Silly Old Bear “Pooh, promise you won’t forget about me, ever. Not even when I’m a hundred,” Christopher Robin implores his bear in the final chapter of AA Milne’s The House at Pooh Corner. This week Winnie-the-Pooh himself turned 100, and he certainly hasn’t been forgotten. Birthday celebrations have included a week of special programmes , introduced by the queen, on Radio 4; a collection of Royal Mail stamps ; and a Google doodle . Not bad for “a bear of very little brain” who appeared in four slim books. Winnie-the-Pooh, illustrated by EH Shepard, was published on 14 October 1926 and had sold 150,000 copies in the US by the end of the year. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I’m bored when I’m not riding’: Billy Loughnane on drive that made him champion jockey at 20
data.description: Flat racing’s youngest champion jockey in more than a century on his relentless – and rapid – journey to the top Billy Loughnane’s mum wanted him to be a vet. “You’d have to ask her why,” he says with a smile that is rarely more than a second or two away. “I’d say money and an easier lifestyle, but I always wanted to be a jockey and made it very clear that was what I wanted to be doing. My parents and family have all been very supportive since.” It seems fair to say that Loughnane’s career choice was the right one. At Ascot on Saturday, the 20-year-old will be officially installed as Flat racing’s new champion jockey and the youngest in more than a century. Pat Eddery was 22 when he won his first title, Frankie Dettori was 23, while Lester Piggott – who rode his first winner at the age of 12 – was twice that age when he landed his first championship. data.title: Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal
data.description: Landslide blocks river and triggers downstream flooding, while summer temperatures persist in Portugal Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged. After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mind
data.description: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fiction At 20, Antonia Susan Byatt was not yet sure she could write. “Do I take myself seriously as a writer?” she asked herself in her diary in September 1956. “No, I think not.” The young Byatt – who would go on to become one of Britain’s most celebrated writers, best known for her 1990 novel Possession: A Romance – was troubled by the possibility that her mind might not be equal to her ambitions. Yet her determination was already evident. On her 20th birthday, she wrote: “Today, I know I can do anything. But not yet.” Continue reading...

data.description: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases. Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. Continue reading...

data.title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting
data.description: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it. After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle. Continue reading...

data.title: Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper
data.description: A ‘family’ of criminals attempt to steal the Mona Lisa from the Louvre in pulpy and forgettable thriller In the last half-decade Stanley Tucci has been a source of near-inexhaustible on- screen delight, whether making friends with nonnas in his delightful cooking shows or smartly judged supporting turns in Conclave and The Devil Wears Prada 2 . He is an actor well placed for a star vehicle of his own, and this one, Masterplan , sounds good on paper: an art heist fronted by the actor at his most debonair, flanked by a grandson of a French New Wave legend (Victor Belmondo, related to Breathless star Jean-Paul) and a buzzy breakout of The White Lotus (Simona Tabasco, winning in season two of Mike White’s comedy). There’s a good bit of pulpy fun to have here, with double, triple and quadruple crossing, silly spy gadgetry which has been updated to include retina scan cloning and something called “VR intrusion”. As British criminal mastermind Roger, Tucci is game to send up aristo archetypes, even if his character often veers into parody. “I’m English,” his character says at one point. “‘Not bad’ is what I say when I orgasm.” Continue reading...

data.title: Look Back review – Kore-eda’s ode to friendship, manga and artistic success
data.description: Two obsessive artists team up to achieve their dreams, but then their aspirations diverge Hirokazu Kore-eda’s sad and beautiful film is about friendship, about the ecstasy and burden of success and about what it means to have an artistic vocation, especially when that vocation is pursued collaboratively, with your best friend. It is adapted by Kore-eda from the standalone, or “one-shot”, online manga story of the same title by Tatsuki Fujimoto, which has in fact already had an anime movie adaptation. Fujino, played by Furi Nanase as a 13-year-old and later by Natsuki Deguchi, is a dedicated would-be manga artist who dreams of being published and adapted for the movies. It is her personal and artistic destiny to come into contact, in her early teens, with fellow manga obsessive Kyomoto, who is played first by Rokka Okada and then as an adult by Aju Makita. Theirs is a kind of platonic but passionate love story. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween
data.description: The comedy smash is back – and now the standups aren’t allowed to laugh or shriek! Lou Sanders, Tom Allen, Phil Wang and more reveal what made them crack – and what happened when they went too far What could be more disorientating for a comedian than not being able to laugh – for nine hours! – nor elicit laughter from anyone else in the room? I’ll tell you. Try all of the above on a sunny summer weekend while pretending it’s Halloween. Then force the comics to return to the scene of what one of their number, Phil Wang, calls “a cross between a gameshow and a psychological experiment”, and relive the whole ordeal for a man from the Guardian. Is it any wonder Wang, Lou Sanders, Tom Allen and others come across as a little punch-drunk 24 hours after emerging from televised captivity on the smash comedy hit Last One Laughing? It’s the day after filming, at Elstree Studios, the show’s Halloween special which sees a unique tweak to its winning formula: contestants must not only refrain from laughter but from screaming. “Which I thought might be a non-event,” says Wang, “but it’s actually harder. I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am.” The participating comics – including paranormal obsessive Daisy May Cooper and that maestro of comedy-horror, Reece Shearsmith – seek not only to amuse each other but spook them too. Which makes sense, says host Jimmy Carr. “Laughs and screams come from the same place. There’s surprise in a joke, and there’s surprise in a jump scare. Comedy and horror mess around in the same area. It’s the same bit of your brain.” Continue reading...

data.title: The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fans
data.description: The lore of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, once bought by Martin Shkreli, is explored in a rambling film produced by RZA For every reason except one, Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, the seventh album by the Wu-Tang Clan , should’ve been a commercial hit. The 31-track double album, recorded in secret between 2007 and 2013, reunited all of the remaining members of the hallowed Staten Island rap crew and featured eye-catching collaborators from the standard (Redman, offshoot group Wu-Tang Killa Bees) to the unexpected (Cher, Game of Thrones actor Carice van Houten). The sound, at least according to those involved, harkened back to the glory days of the group’s beginnings in the 90s. But for years, almost no one heard it. The group only issued a single copy of Once Upon a Time in Shaolin – on CD, ensconced within layers of filigreed silver – with the stipulation, in legalese, that it could not be used for any commercial purposes for 88 years. The decree, either a stunt or a bold artistic statement on streaming’s devaluation of music, depending on your generosity and perhaps your net worth, succeeded in drumming up plenty of hype. And if you were anywhere around the blogosphere or cable news in 2015, you may recall that the beneficiary of that hype – the purchaser and thus single intended listener of this $2m musical treasure – was one Martin Shkreli , the “pharma bro” widely despised for gleefully hiking the costs of prescription drugs for profit. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?
data.description: Once scrappy post-punk poets, they’re now one of the biggest bands in the world. As they release new album Dopamine Chamber, fans including Kneecap and Shame explain their sensational rise When Irish rockers Fontaines DC emerged in 2019, they were a bunch of post-punk poets making abrasive guitar music at a time when Dance Monkey , Drake and The Greatest Showman reigned supreme. But today, as their fifth album Dopamine Chamber is released, the quintet are looking towards a 2027 filled with gigs in UK stadiums, US arenas and headline slots at big European festivals – plus rumours of topping Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage. It’s quite a trajectory. Their rise has been strangely traditional for a time when social media has culture in a chokehold. Ever more ambitious albums, the support of radio and institutions such as the BBC, and a lot of touring have all played parts. Beyond that, “fact is, they’re one of the best bands in the world,” says fellow countryman Mo Chara, one third of Kneecap . Continue reading...

data.title: PatKop & Say album review – playfulness and beguiling delicacy in mix of new and old
data.description: Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazil Say (Alpha ) Compositions by both musicians themselves frame works by Szymanowski and Prokofiev Patricia Kopatchinskaja and Fazil Say have recorded Say’s music together before, but this is their first recording to feature Kopatchinskaja as a composer as well, but this is no vanity project: Say’s and Kopatchinskaja’s pieces make good complements to Szymanowski’s three Mythes and Prokofiev’s Violin Sonata No 1. Say’s Lost Screams Sonata is driven by repeated piano rhythms, its fierceness tempered by an episode in which Kopatchinskaja plays low, ghostly harmonics and Say gently plucks the strings of the piano so it almost sounds like a second violin. Kopatchinskaja’s three-movement piece UniSolo is an impish work with a searching, thoughtful playfulness that comes from the parallel world to the Kurtág miniatures she plays so well. data.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
data.description: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo The Heights by Ian Rankin (Orion, £25) Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to novelists. Rankin’s first standalone thriller in almost two decades centres on The Heights, 18 storeys high and facing London’s Hyde Park, where DS Gillian Gish is investigating the suspicious death of night-shift security guard Dwayne Hogarth. The high-net-worth individuals who live there, including a young singer, a gangster’s wife, a man who “made a mint in post-glasnost Russia” and the daughter of a very well-connected Zimbabwean, are either uncontactable or tight-lipped, and it soon becomes clear that the developer, despite his bravado, is in financial trouble. Everyone, it appears, has something to hide – and then a second corpse is discovered. Rankin is a superb storyteller, and this is well up to his usual high standard, while DS Gish – less complex, but considerably more relatable than John Rebus – is worthy of her own series. The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld & Justine Larbalestier (Viking, £18.99) There are shades of both The Sopranos and Wednesday Addams in this tale of a powerful old American family whose trade is murder, blackmail and financial fraud. As the Mortons’ great hope, Jessica, puts it, “Give your child a strong hand, a sharp knife, and a big family, then teach them loyalty without care.” The children are given pet rabbits on which to prove their lack of compassion; the family are as ruthless with their own as with everyone else, their graveyard being full of youngsters who failed to make the grade. Jessica, who achieved her first kill aged 20, looks set to take on the murderous mantle, but a summer internship leads to a train of events that culminate in the discovery of a conscience. The Mortons is vivid and exciting, with a nice vein of mordant humour, but there’s a lot of world-building to get through, some of it lacking in internal logic; it’s hard to keep track of the many characters, and the violence towards innocent people and animals may leave some readers feeling queasy. data.translatedDescription: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian Slovo The Heights by Ian Rankin (Orion, £25) Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to novelists. Rankin’s first standalone thriller in almost two decades centres on The Heights, 18 storeys high and facing London’s Hyde Park, where DS Gillian Gish is investigating the suspicious death of night-shift security guard Dwayne Hogarth. The high-net-worth individuals who live there, including a young singer, a gangster’s wife, a man who “made a mint in post-glasnost Russia” and the daughter of a very well-connected Zimbabwean, are either uncontactable or tight-lipped, and it soon becomes clear that the developer, despite his bravado, is in financial trouble. Everyone, it appears, has something to hide – and then a second corpse is discovered. Rankin is a superb storyteller, and this is well up to his usual high standard, while DS Gish – less complex, but considerably more relatable than John Rebus – is worthy of her own series. The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld & Justine Larbalestier (Viking, £18.99) There are shades of both The Sopranos and Wednesday Addams in this tale of a powerful old American family whose trade is murder, blackmail and financial fraud. As the Mortons’ great hope, Jessica, puts it, “Give your child a strong hand, a sharp knife, and a big family, then teach them loyalty without care.” The children are given pet rabbits on which to prove their lack of compassion; the family are as ruthless with their own as with everyone else, their graveyard being full of youngsters who failed to make the grade. Jessica, who achieved her first kill aged 20, looks set to take on the murderous mantle, but a summer internship leads to a train of events that culminate in the discovery of a conscience. The Mortons is vivid and exciting, with a nice vein of mordant humour, but there’s a lot of world-building to get through, some of it lacking in internal logic; it’s hard to keep track of the many characters, and the violence towards innocent people and animals may leave some readers feeling queasy. data.title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors
data.description: PC; Origame Digital This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears A Nazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape. For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘She asked me to lie on her feet while she did sit-ups’: your memories of Esther Rantzen
data.description: From inspiring careers to treating people to unforgettable curries, the late presenter and campaigner had quite the impact on Guardian readers. Colleagues, admirers and TV show guests share their stories The summer of 1976 held a particularly fond memory for my family. In one episode of her programme The Big Time, my father took part in conducting the Royal Philharmonic in Croydon and met several of his musical idols. Esther and her team visited our home, causing much teenage excitement, took us for lunch at a local Indian restaurant (the height of sophistication) and after lunch asked me to sit on her feet in our back garden while she did sit-ups. We were kids, probably in the way of filming, but were included and treated warmly and impressed by her down-to-earth manner. We fondly remember the visit and as Dad said at the end of the film: “lovely Esther”. I’m glad she went on to make so many important contributions to the lives of so many. Rosalind Cresswell, Maine, USA Continue reading...

data.title: The Penelopiad review – move over, Odysseus! Margaret Atwood lets Penelope’s maids run riot
data.description: York Theatre Royal Atwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threads After a summer of Odysseus hogging the spotlight thanks to Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster take on Homer, it’s time for the women to have their say. The Penelopiad is, as its title declares, the story of Odysseus’s famously faithful wife. But in Margaret Atwood’s play, adapted for the stage from her own novella, it is also Penelope’s brutally slain maids whose perspective is reclaimed. If Penelope’s voice has been sidelined, theirs have been silenced altogether. The backdrop for this revisionist storytelling is hades. In Sara Perks’s minimal design, it’s a sterile, featureless place, deliberately drained of the passion and mess of life. Thick, blood-red ropes suggest the strands – literal and narrative – woven by Penelope and the cords used to hang the maids. These wronged figures form a chorus, acting out episodes from Penelope’s life as well as interrupting with their own bitter take on events. We hear of Penelope and Odysseus’s marriage, his departure to Troy, and the long, long years that followed. Continue reading...

data.title: Decluttering your online life: how to get your digital house in order and protect your data from AI
data.description: The average person spends 40% of their waking hours online. Clearing out digital clutter can minimise environmental impacts and boost productivity Change by degrees offers life hacks and sustainable living tips each Saturday to help reduce your household’s carbon footprint Got a question or tip for reducing household emissions? Email us at changebydegrees@theguardian.com Many Australians worry about datacentres swallowing up local land and energy but we rarely look closely at our own digital trails. Our endless photo and video streams, bursting inboxes and unread subscriptions all feed the appetite for ever growing digital infrastructure. The average person spends 40% of their waking hours online – browsing the web or social media, streaming music or videos, or communicating – producing the equivalent of 229kg of carbon emissions, a study in Nature Communications found. And using AI tools and chatbots to generate text, images or video consumes “orders of magnitude” more energy than traditional computing methods. Continue reading...

data.title: Texas courthouse vacant since 1977 faces demolition after $120 million repair estimates

While some historical artifacts will be saved, extensive asbestos contamination complicates the safe removal process.

data.title: China bar exam row sinks Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia after just 5 days
data.description:
Katie Zacharia was “let go” as White House press secretary on Friday, a White House official said, five days into a tenure dominated by questions over her claimed legal career in China, where she said she had passed a bar exam.

data.title: Sua empresa tem planejamento estratégico, e você?
data.description: Toda virada de ciclo, o ritual se repete nas empresas . Revisamos metas, discutimos orçamento, desenhamos cenários de expansão e, nas organizações mais maduras, falamos de sucessão. Nenhuma empresa entra em um novo ano sem saber para onde quer ir, com quais recursos e em quanto tempo. Curioso é que o mesmo empresário, tão rigoroso com a planilha, raramente aplica esse método à própria vida. A saúde fica para depois da próxima entrega. O casamento, para as férias que nunca chegam inteiras. Os filhos, para o fim de semana em que o celular, quem sabe, ficará esquecido por alguns momentos . E o tempo, único recurso que não se recompra, é gasto sem orçamento algum. Aprendi, ao longo dos anos à frente de negócios bilionários, uma ideia simples que mudou a forma como organizo minha rotina: o CPF sustenta o CNPJ. Leia mais (10/16/2026 - 23h00)

data.title: »Jeg står nu nede i den her blindgyde, helt rasende, og ved simpelthen ikke, hvordan jeg skal komme ud«
data.description: Med sin satire over strukturel sexisme har Maren Uthaug antændt en stor, usædvanlig engageret fanskare, der hækler, broderer og støber gaver til hende eller ligefrem bliver tatoveret. Nu går hun live landet over for at møde dem ansigt til ansigt, så de sammen kan være flammerøde af vrede og have det seriøst sjovt. Og hun har opdaget, at hun kan bruge sin vrede terapeutisk.

data.title: AI w szkole nie kusi jak owoc zakazany. To owoc nisko wiszący. I w tym problem
data.description: Nie wchodzi się dwa razy do tej samej rzeki, ale okazuje się, że można próbować dwakroć do niej wrzucić dzieci. Kiedy w jednym kącie szkoły próbujemy ratować osoby zniszczone przez smartficę i bigtechowe platformy, z drugiego już wyłazi pokusa, żeby przetestować na uczniach sztuczną inteligencję.

data.title: Słynny hotel w Nowym Jorku zamyka się na kilka lat. Nadchodzi wielki remont
data.description: Plaza Hotel na nowojorskim Manhattanie to jedna z architektonicznych ikon Nowego Jorku i symboli tego miasta. Obiekt niebawem przerwie działalność – konieczny jest gruntowny remont jednego z najbardziej prestiżowych hoteli w Nowym Jorku. Przerwa potrwa co najmniej cztery lata.

data.title: Nákladní automobil se na Jablonecku zaklínil mezi svodidly a zablokoval silnici

data.title: Cizinci v Boleslavi tvoří čtvrtinu obyvatel, v Praze třetinu. Sílí obavy o bezpečnost
data.description: Necítíme se bezpečně. Opakující se názor lidí jak v průzkumech, tak v diskusích na sociálních sítích v Mladé Boleslavi. Například podle posledního průzkumu, který si zadalo město, se bezpečně necítí až 63 procent dotázaných.

data.title: Žlutá, nebo šedá obálka? Tsoukernik u voleb zaskočila barva. Hlas ale může platit
data.description: Nečekané pozdvižení vyvolala fotografie kandidátky hnutí ANO do Senátu Sandry Tsoukernik, která při hlasování vhazovala do volební urny žlutou obálku. Sama politička si přitom podle svých slov neobvyklé barvy vůbec nevšimla. Pro iDNES.cz uvedla, že obálku dostala přímo od volební komise a o její barvě začala přemýšlet až zpětně.

data.title: Střelec na škole v Oregonu byl jejím bývalým žákem. Zabil tři děti a učitele
data.description: Šestnáctiletý střelec, který ve čtvrtek na základní škole v oregonském městě Bend zabil tři děti a jednoho učitele, byl bývalým žákem této instituce. V pátek to uvedl šéf místní policie Mike Krantz s tím, že mladík při útoku použil brokovnici, z níž vystřelil patnáctkrát.

data.title: Řídit si svou spotřebu elektřiny bude do budoucna snazší, říká šéf ČEZ Distribuce
data.description: Solární a větrné elektrárny, bateriová úložiště i velké průmyslové provozy zvyšují tlak na českou distribuční síť. V některých místech už její kapacita nestačí a investice do připojování nových zdrojů prudce rostou, říká Martin Zmelík, generální ředitel ČEZ Distribuce.

data.title: Trhal lístky na Ondříčkův film a v jednom nyní hraje. Splněný sen, říká Vodochodský
data.description: Herec Vojtěch Vodochodský je jednou z hvězd nejnovějšího filmu Davida Ondříčka Kluci to vidí jinak než holky. Generační snímek označovaný za komedii může svým názvem podle mladého herce na první pohled mást. Se svou postavou Davida se podle vlastních slov ztotožňuje, rozhodně však oproti němu nevidí svět přes růžové brýle.

data.title: Sokol dostane zpět pět milionů z peněz, o které přišel kvůli podvodu zaměstnankyně
data.description: České obci sokolské policie vrátí pět milionů korun, o které přišla v souvislosti s podvodem, při němž bývalá zaměstnankyně připravila organizaci o desítky milionů korun, a které policie zajistila ženě na účtech. Serveru iROZHLAS.cz to řekli policejní mluvčí Jan Daněk a starosta České obce sokolské Martin Chlumský.

data.title: NKÚ nabere 16 nových zaměstnanců kvůli ostraze budovy. O policejní ochranu přišel
data.description: Nejvyšší kontrolní úřad (NKÚ) zřídí od příštího roku kvůli ostraze svého sídla 16 nových pracovních míst. Půjde o 15 míst pro pracovníky ochrany budovy a jedno místo jejich vedoucího. Příslušnou změnu platového řádu, která to umožní, schválil v pondělí sněmovní rozpočtový výbor. Mluvčí NKÚ Hana Kadečková sdělila, že peníze na nové lidi úřad vyčleněné nemá a bude je muset vzít z provozních výdajů.

data.title: Německé železnici ujíždí moderní doba. Vlaky totiž brzdí stoletá technika
data.description: Ještě donedávna hlídala trasy vlaků mezi Mnichovem a rakouskými hranicemi signalizační stanice zřízená v roce 1899. Na konci loňského roku ale společnost Deutsche Bahn 126 let staré zařízení v Mühldorfu am Inn vyměnila za elektronický systém. Propast mezi stárnoucí železniční infrastrukturou a moderními vlaky je ovšem stále patrná.

data.title: Unese vojáka i s výstrojí. Ukrajinci ukázali evakuační drony
data.description: Ukrajinská společnost SkyFall vyrábějící bezpilotní letouny představila drony, které jsou určené k evakuaci raněných vojáků z fronty. Pokud se technologie osvědčí, bude s její pomocí možné dostat se k raněným, ke kterým pozemní vozidla nemají přístup. Drony mohou zachránit vojáky, pro které je přežití otázkou hodin.

data.title: Každý jedenáctý novorozenec je cizinec. Jejich počet i podíl se za deset let znásobil
data.description: Zhruba každé jedenácté dítě, které se loni v Česku narodilo, nemělo české občanství. Před deseti lety to bylo každé třicáté dítě. Oba rodiče ze zahraničí mělo v minulém roce 7249 narozených chlapců a děvčat. Počet se za posledních deset let zdvojnásobil. V Praze tvořili malí cizinci a cizinky loni pak téměř čtvrtinu narozených.

data.title: Víno zraje v zakopaných nádobách. Sklepmistra z Roudnice inspirovala stará Gruzie
data.description: V zakopaných hliněných nádobách v areálu roudnického zámku zraje už druhá úroda z místní vinice. Jde o tradiční metodu výroby vína z Gruzie, tato technika je stará už tisíce let. V nádobách zvaných kvevri víno vzniká a zraje přirozeným způsobem. Na sever Čech tradici přivezl Karel Stejskal, sklepmistr Vinařství Zámek Lobkowicz Roudnice.

data.title: Volby 2026 ONLINE: Češi si druhý den vybírají nové senátory
data.description: Voliči v části Česka v sobotu dokončí letošní obměnu třetiny Senátu. K pěti kandidátům, kteří uspěli už v prvním kole před týdnem, přibude dalších 22 senátorů. Lidé mohou volit do 14 hodin, poté začnou volební komise sčítat hlasy. Během odpoledne už bude jasné, kdo získá šestiletý mandát v horní komoře Parlamentu.

data.title: Výsledky voleb 2026: kdo ovládne Senát?
data.description: Češi v pátek a sobotu vybírají své kandidáty ve druhém kole senátních voleb, na rozdíl od toho prvního pouze ve 22 obvodech z původních 27. V pěti obvodech totiž zvítězili kandidáti už v prvním kole se ziskem přes 50 procent odevzdaných hlasů, což je vyrovnaný rekord senátních voleb. Volební místnosti jsou otevřeny do dnešních 14:00, pak začne sčítání.

data.title: Třídí špulky, tkají osnovy. Vyhořelé textilní dílně vracejí tvář bývalí zaměstnanci
data.description: Regály se plní knihami se vzorky i přízemi a špulkami nití, na tkalcovské stavy se vracejí osnovy i části tkanin. Historicky cenná vzorkovna někdejší textilky Karnola v Krnově se dál vzpamatovává z ničivého požáru. Do dílny se opět vrátili její bývalí zaměstnanci, aby prostor co nejvíce přiblížili podobě, v níž za běžného provozu fungoval.

data.title: Hrobník už má trať na lopatě. Rušenou mladotickou lokálku má nahradit stezka
data.description: Už posedmé vyrazí v sobotu turisté na neobvyklý pochod podél 13 kilometrů dlouhého úseku železniční trati z Kralovic do Mladotic na  Plzeňsku. Poslední vlak tu zdolával velké stoupání od Mladotic k Trojanům s množstvím přejezdů na konci roku 1996. Většina kolejí je na opuštěné trati už rozkradená. Krátký úsek trati se má obnovit, zbytek proměnit v turistickou stezku.

data.title: Sázkovým kurzům věří víc než průzkumům. Američané udělali z voleb politické kasino
data.description: Do kongresových voleb zbývají necelé tři týdny. V médiích se mluví o demokratickém tsunami, prezident Trump totiž ztrácí podporu. Aby Amerika v tom politickém dusnu a napětí mohla vůbec dýchat, musela si vymyslet, jak se pobavit. A tak na politiky sází jako na koně. Není to však jen zábava. V předchozích volbách se ukázalo, že sázkové kurzy byly přesnější než předvolební průzkumy.

data.title: Čína zaplavuje svět levným masem. Kuřata poráží rychleji, konkurence se bojí
data.description: Čínští producenti masa a mléčných výrobků hledají odbyt v zahraničí. Díky státním dotacím, moderním technologiím a nízkým cenám získávají podíl na světových trzích, zatímco doma slábne poptávka. Jejich expanze znepokojuje evropské i asijské konkurenty a může přinést další obchodní spory.

data.title: Trumpova mluvčí bleskově končí. Bude jí líp, řekl prezident
data.description: Americký prezident Donald Trump v pátek naznačil, že jeho nová mluvčí Katie Zachariaová ve funkci brzy skončí. Podle agentury AP přitom už po necelém týdnu z Bílého domu odchází. Kritiku vyvolal její první tiskový brífink, během něhož většinu úvodního projevu četla z papíru. Média navíc začala zpochybňovat její právnickou kvalifikaci.

data.title: Svět podle Putina: ofenziva zrychluje, dobytí Donbasu je na dosah
data.description: Rusko v ofenzivě výrazně zrychlilo, prohlásil ruský prezident Vladimir Putin. Ruská armáda od počátku roku dobyla přibližně 310 obcí a 6500 kilometrů čtverečních ukrajinského území, uvedl v pátek. Putinova tvrzení jsou v rozporu s dostupnými údaji o územních ziscích ruské armády, jejíž postup na východě Ukrajiny se letos zpomalil.

data.title: Volby 2026 ONLINE: Češi si vybírají nové senátory. Účast nepřekvapila
data.description: V části Česka se dnes ve dvě hodiny odpoledne opět otevřely volební místnosti. Lidé vybírají celkem 22 senátorů. Zástupci hnutí STAN mohou po šesti letech zopakovat své vítězství. Svého favorita podpořil předseda hnutí Vít Rakušan, který volil stejně jako v prvním kole Michaela Kašpara. Ministr zahraničí Petr Macinka (Motoristé sobě) k urně dorazil s téměř dvouhodinovým zpožděním.

data.title: Stav papeže Lva XIV. se po operaci se lepší, mluvil s Putinem
data.description: Papež Lev XIV., který se zotavuje po úterní operaci, v pátek mluvil po telefonu s ruským prezidentem Vladimirem Putinem. Oznámil to v pátek odpoledne Vatikán, který zveřejnil první fotografie papeže po operaci. Lékaři zároveň oznámili, že výsledky potvrzují pokračující zlepšování jeho zdravotního stavu. Papež zůstává zatím v nemocnici, kde mu lékaři odstranili část pravé plíce.

data.title: Trumpova dohoda o naftě s Putinem škodí Evropě, dělá to kvůli volbám, míní Babiš
data.description: Český premiér Andrej Babiš se domnívá, že americký prezident Donald Trump podniká některé kroky kvůli volbám, které se budou v listopadu konat v USA. Dohoda o dodávkách ruské nafty, kterou Trump uzavřel s ruským prezidentem Vladimirem Putinem, podle Babiše poškozuje pozici Evropy i v souvislosti s válkou na Ukrajině. Český premiér to řekl v pátek po skončení summitu v Bruselu v reakci na otázku, zda po posledních Trumpových krocích změnil názor na jeho schopnost ukončit válku na Ukrajině.

data.title: Neúspěšný senátní kandidát Přísahy si řekl o peníze za podporu soupeře z ANO
data.description: Neúspěšný senátní kandidát Přísahy Pavel Černý si řekl o 50 tisíc korun za to, že podpoří v druhém kole senátních voleb na Znojemsku Jiřího Kyněru za ANO. Peníze nedostal. Podporu vyjádřil protikandidátovi Tomáši Třetinovi z TOP 09. Černý potvrdil, že peníze skutečně chtěl, a to jako kompenzaci za to, že bude natáčet videa a vystupovat jako influencer v Kyněrův prospěch.

data.title: Organizações pedem ao Governo para se opor a cortes na ciência no próximo orçamento da UE
data.description: Seis organizações ligadas à ciência e inovação apelaram ao Governo para se opor à redução de verbas prevista no próximo orçamento comunitário para essa área e para defender um financiamento 220 mil milhões de euros até 2034.

data.title: EU-GCC: Energy security, diversification of sources cornerstone of economic stability and sustainable development

The participants also urged for a renewed focus on a comprehensive free trade agreement to strengthen economic ties.

data.title: Palestinian factions agree in Cairo on a national dialogue conference; Fatah hints at bringing forward the election date

data.title: Pakistan says attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure ‘worrying’ for outlook

The government is focusing on fiscal reforms to enhance tax revenues and has emphasized efforts to combat tax theft.

data.title: Banques burundaises : des liquidités sous pression, de la hausse des crédits impayés
data.description: Les banques commerciales opérant au Burundi font face à un manque criant de liquidités alimenté notamment par la thésaurisation des ménages et la hausse des crédits non performants. Cette situation complique leur capacité à honorer leurs engagements envers les déposants et suscite des interrogations sur la stabilité du système bancaire. Dans son analyse, l’économiste Jean Ndenzako revient sur les causes profondes de ces tensions de liquidité, les risques qu’elles font peser sur les banques et leurs clients ainsi que les mesures qui permettraient d’y remédier.

data.title: dLocal et Western Union élargissent leur partenariat aux paiements de transferts d’argent (payouts) au Cameroun
data.description: © PARTENAIRE Le Cameroun est le premier marché à bénéficier de cette extension, qui s'appuie sur le partenariat d'encaissement (collections) déjà en place entre les deux entreprises. dLocal, la plateforme de paiement de référence qui connecte les commerçants du monde entier aux marchés émergents, et Western Union, un leader mondial du transfert d'argent transfrontalier, ont annoncé l'extension de leur partenariat en Afrique aux décaissements (payouts). Cette extension vient compléter le travail d'encaissement que les deux entreprises mènent déjà ensemble : dLocal fournit la couche technologique et de connectivité, tandis que des partenaires locaux agréés exécutent les services de paiement et de décaissement concernés. L'expansion débutera par un corridor de décaissement opérationnel au Cameroun. Un parcours plus fiable, de bout en bout Ce nouveau chapitre du partenariat offre aux bénéficiaires de transferts d'argent sur les marchés africains un moyen plus rapide et plus fiable de recevoir des fonds, via les moyens de paiement locaux qu'ils utilisent déjà au quotidien. Au Cameroun, l'un des marchés les plus fragmentés de la région et fondé sur les portefeuilles électroniques, les bénéficiaires pourront recevoir leurs transferts directement dans les portefeuilles locaux pris en charge, par l'intermédiaire de partenaires de décaissement locaux opérant dans le cadre des réglementations locales applicables (opérateurs de réseaux mobiles ou institutions financières). Cela comble une lacune qui leur laissait jusqu'ici peu d'options fiables. La fiabilité sur laquelle les expéditeurs de transferts comptent déjà s'étend désormais jusqu'au bénéficiaire, créant un parcours unique et fiable de l'envoi à la réception. Cette extension renforce également les bases permettant à Western Union de s'appuyer sur un partenaire unique pour l'encaissement comme pour le décaissement, soutenant ainsi la croissance continue des corridors de transferts numériques sur les marchés émergents. « Chez Western Union, notre priorité est toujours de faire en sorte que nos clients reçoivent leur argent de manière fiable et fluide, où qu'ils se trouvent », a déclaré Mohamed Touhami El Ouazzani, Vice-Président régional et Responsable Afrique chez Western Union. « Étendre notre collaboration avec dLocal aux décaissements nous permet d'offrir cette même fiabilité côté réception, en commençant par des marchés comme le Cameroun. » « L'encaissement et le décaissement ont toujours été traités comme deux problèmes distincts », a déclaré Agustin Botta, Responsable EMEA chez dLocal. « Résoudre la moitié d'un transfert, c'est laisser la moitié du problème entière. Avec Western Union, nous travaillons ensemble à combler cet écart, en construisant un parcours plus cohérent de l'envoi à la réception. » dLocal construit l'infrastructure financière des marchés de demain, en connectant les grandes entreprises mondiales à des milliards de consommateurs des marchés émergents en Amérique latine, en Afrique, en Asie et au Moyen-Orient. Grâce à la plateforme « One dLocal », les entreprises peuvent accepter des paiements, effectuer des décaissements et régler des fonds à l'échelle mondiale, sans avoir à gérer des intégrations fragmentées ni des entités locales. Western Union s'engage à aider les personnes du monde entier qui aspirent à construire un avenir financier pour elles-mêmes, leurs proches et leurs communautés. Les institutions leaders du transfert d'argent transfrontalier et multidevises, des paiements et des services financiers numériques permettent aux consommateurs, aux entreprises, aux institutions financières et aux gouvernements, dans plus de 200 pays et territoires et plus de 130 devises, de se connecter à des milliards de comptes bancaires, des millions de portefeuilles électroniques et de cartes, ainsi qu'à un réseau mondial de centaines de milliers de points de vente. Au-delà du Cameroun À l'avenir, les deux entreprises envisagent d'étendre le décaissement à d'autres marchés africains, notamment le Nigeria, avec des virements bancaires et des portefeuilles électroniques, dans le cadre d'une volonté plus large de couvrir l'ensemble du parcours du transfert sur un plus grand nombre de marchés émergents. Les marchés émergents sont à un tournant pour les transferts d'argent, les bénéficiaires attendant de plus en plus, à la réception, la même rapidité et la même fiabilité que celles dont les expéditeurs ont l'habitude. La Banque mondiale estime que les flux de transferts d'argent vers l'Afrique subsaharienne ont atteint environ 57 milliards de dollars US en 2024, ce qui rappelle l'importance de ces fonds pour les ménages qui les attendent. dLocal et Western Union y voient une étape supplémentaire dans la construction de cette fiabilité, corridor après corridor. Cet article dLocal et Western Union élargissent leur partenariat aux paiements de transferts d’argent (payouts) au Cameroun est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroun : Paul Biya nomme Remy Nama, nouveau président du Conseil constitutionnel
data.description: © DR Par décrets, le président Paul Biya nomme, ce 16 octobre 2026, Remy Nama, successeur de Clément Atangana à la présidence du Conseil constitutionnel, et Abdoulaye Daouda, nouveau membre dudit conseil en remplacement de Bah Oumarou Sanda. Ça Y est, le nouveau président du Conseil constitutionnel du Cameroun est connu. Le président Paul Biya vient de rendre public deux décrets nommant aux deux postes vacants à la juridiction constitutionnelle, plus haute juridiction en matière électorale. Remy Nama est donc à compter de ce 16 octobre 2026, le nouveau et le deuxième président de l’histoire du Conseil constitutionnel, institution créée en 1996 et mise en fonction depuis février 2018. Magistrat hors hiérarchie, Remy Nama a servi comme entre autres comme chargé de mission au secrétariat général de la présidence de la République ; il a siégé comme au conseil d’administration du Parc national de matériel de génie civil (Matgenie). Il a aussi été membre du conseil d’administration représentant la présidence de la République à l’Agence de promotion des petites et moyennes entreprises (APME). Le nouveau président du Conseil a été nommé ce jour dans un autre décret comme membre du Conseil constitutionnel avec Abdoulaye Daouda. Nommé récemment conseiller spécial du président du Sénat Abdoulaye Daouda est le nouveau membre du Conseil constitutionnel désigné par le président de l’Assemblée nationale en remplacement du membre Bah Oumarou Sanda décédé en août 2026. Ainsi s’achève le processus de remplacement du président du Conseil constitutionnel et du membre décédés. Il reste à présent la prestation de serment pour le début effectif de leurs missions au conseil des sages. Cet article Cameroun : Paul Biya nomme Remy Nama, nouveau président du Conseil constitutionnel est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroon International Tech Summit : l’UNESCO arrime la tech à l’inclusion
data.description: © DR La deuxième édition du Cameroon International Tech Summit 2026 s'est ouverte le 15 octobre au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé sous la présidence de la Ministre des Postes et Télécommunications, Minette Libom Li Likeng. Placée sous le thème "The Bold Agenda", la rencontre a vu la participation remarquée de l'UNESCO, venue rappeler que l'innovation n'a de sens que si elle sert l'éducation, la culture et le développement durable. Yaoundé a vibré au rythme de l'innovation. La deuxième édition du Cameroon International Tech Summit (CITS26), organisée par Mountain Hub, a officiellement ouvert ses portes le 15 octobre au Palais des Congrès. Présidée par la Ministre Minette Libom Li Likeng, la cérémonie d'ouverture a réuni professionnels des TIC, entrepreneurs, jeunes innovateurs et partenaires internationaux autour d'une ambition commune : accélérer le développement durable en mobilisant le potentiel de la jeunesse camerounaise. Pendant trois jours, le sommet offre une plateforme d'échanges entre secteurs public et privé, pour présenter des solutions innovantes et nouer des partenariats structurants pour la transformation numérique du Cameroun. Dans cette effervescence technologique, l'UNESCO a marqué les esprits. À travers un stand d'exposition dédié, l'Organisation a présenté sa mission et sa contribution dans ses domaines de compétence : l'éducation, la science, la culture, la communication et l'information. Plus qu'une simple exposition, c'est un message fort qui a été délivré : le progrès technologique doit être arrimé à la construction de sociétés inclusives et durables. Par sa présence, l'UNESCO s'est inscrite dans la dynamique d'innovation du CITS26, tout en soulignant le rôle central de la connaissance, de la créativité, de l'accès à une information fiable et de la coopération internationale pour une innovation au service de la société. Une participation qui rappelle que derrière les algorithmes et les start-up, l'enjeu reste humain : faire progresser l'éducation, favoriser la coopération scientifique et sauvegarder le patrimoine culturel. Cet article Cameroon International Tech Summit : l’UNESCO arrime la tech à l’inclusion est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Financements : Louis Paul Motaze séduit les investisseurs à Bangkok
data.description: © DR En marge des Assemblées annuelles du FMI et de la Banque mondiale à Bangkok, le Ministre des Finances, Louis Paul Motaze, a organisé un forum dédié à la situation économique et financière du Cameroun. Bangkok, Thaïlande. Le Cameroun anticipe. En marge des Assemblées annuelles du Fonds Monétaire International et de la Banque Mondiale, le Ministre des Finances, Louis Paul Motaze, a tenu un forum stratégique consacré au Cameroun le 15 octobre 2026. Face à un parterre d'investisseurs et de partenaires financiers, le membre du gouvernement a dressé un tableau de la situation économique et financière du pays, tout en déclinant ses perspectives à moyen terme. L'initiative n'est pas anodine. A un an de l'échéance, Yaoundé veut préparer le terrain pour ses opérations de financement de 2027. Le Ministre a ainsi sollicité l'accompagnement des investisseurs internationaux pour les prochaines levées de fonds destinées à soutenir la croissance. Cette démarche de proactivité vise deux objectifs : maintenir un dialogue permanent et de confiance avec les bailleurs traditionnels, et surtout élargir le cercle des possibilités de mobilisation de ressources. Des ressources indispensables pour financer les priorités de développement définies dans la Stratégie Nationale de Développement SND30, dans un contexte mondial marqué par le resserrement des conditions financières. Par ce forum de Bangkok, Louis Paul Motaze confirme la stratégie du Cameroun : aller chercher les financements là où ils se trouvent, en rassurant sur la solidité de ses fondamentaux économiques. Cet article Financements : Louis Paul Motaze séduit les investisseurs à Bangkok est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Polluants organiques : le Cameroun actualise son arsenal contre 18 nouveaux produits toxiques
data.description: © DR Le ministre de l'Environnement, de la Protection de la Nature et du Développement durable, HELE Pierre, a présidé le 15 octobre 2026 à Yaoundé l'atelier national de validation du Plan National de Mise en œuvre de la Convention de Stockholm. Une actualisation rendue obligatoire par l'article 7 de la Convention, pour intégrer 18 nouvelles substances chimiques hautement dangereuses ajoutées entre 2009 et 2019. Le Cameroun passe à la vitesse supérieure dans la lutte contre la pollution chimique. Face à la menace grandissante des Polluants Organiques Persistants (POP), le gouvernement peaufine sa riposte. Réunis à Yaoundé le 15 octobre 2026 en atelier national de validation, experts, administrations, secteur privé, société civile et partenaires techniques planchent depuis hier sur la version 3 du Plan National de Mise en œuvre (PNM) de la Convention de Stockholm, ratifiée par le Cameroun en 2005. L'enjeu est de taille : intégrer dans la stratégie nationale les 18 nouveaux produits chimiques inscrits aux annexes de la Convention entre 2009 et 2019. Une obligation conventionnelle, mais surtout un impératif de santé publique. Dans son allocution d'ouverture, le Ministre HELE Pierre a été clair : le futur PNM doit être "renforcé, fidèle à la réalité camerounaise et constituer un outil de gestion écologiquement rationnelle". Il a appelé à une vigilance accrue des Mairies, souvent en première ligne face au brûlage à l'air libre des déchets, l'une des principales sources d'émission de POP, et a plaidé pour un renforcement du contrôle et de la législation. Car les POP sont des tueurs silencieux. Ces substances extrêmement toxiques se dégradent lentement, s'accumulent dans les tissus adipeux, voyagent sur de longues distances via l'air et l'eau et contaminent toute la chaîne alimentaire. On les retrouve partout : dans les pesticides agricoles, les équipements électriques, les matériaux de construction, mais aussi dans des objets du quotidien comme les ustensiles de cuisine et les textiles.
